hints: Focus on how Kc units come from concentration units, where each aqueous concentration has units mol dm-3.
Remember solids are left out of the Kc expression, so only count moles of (aq) species on each side to find the change.
Check each equation for (moles of aqueous products minus moles of aqueous reactants) equal to -1, which gives mol-1 dm3.
walkthrough:
**Recall how Kc units work**

Think of each concentration as having units of $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$. The overall units are just what is left after dividing products by reactants.

$$\text{units of } K_c = \frac{(\text{mol dm}^{-3})^{\text{aqueous products}}}{(\text{mol dm}^{-3})^{\text{aqueous reactants}}}$$

**Remember to ignore solids**

Solids like $\text{C(s)}$ have constant concentration and are omitted from Kc. Only (aq) species count.

$$\text{For 1: } K_c = \frac{[\text{D}]}{[\text{A}][\text{B}]}$$

**Test equation 1**

One aqueous product divided by two aqueous reactants gives $(\text{mol dm}^{-3})^{-1}$.

$$\frac{\text{mol dm}^{-3}}{(\text{mol dm}^{-3})^2} = \text{mol}^{-1}\text{dm}^{3}$$ 
So 1 is correct.

**Test equations 2 and 3**

For 2, $K_c = [\text{R}]/([\text{P}][\text{Q}])$, again 1 product over 2 reactants, so same units.

For 3, $K_c = ([\text{Y}][\text{Z}])/([\text{W}][\text{X}]^2)$, that is 2 products over 3 reactants.

$$\frac{(\text{mol dm}^{-3})^2}{(\text{mol dm}^{-3})^3} = \text{mol}^{-1}\text{dm}^{3}$$ 
So 2 and 3 are also correct, meaning 1, 2 and 3 all work.

options.A: Option A states 1, 2 and 3 are all possible. All three have one fewer aqueous product mole than aqueous reactant moles, giving a net power of -1 and units of mol-1 dm3. Equation 1 omits C(s), leaving 1 over 2. Equations 2 and 3 also give 1 over 2 and 2 over 3.
options.B: This suggests only 1 and 2 work. It is tempting if you miscount equation 3 because of the 2X coefficient. But 2 products over 1+2 = 3 reactants still gives (mol dm-3) to the power -1, so 3 should not be excluded.
options.C: This suggests only 2 and 3 work. It is tempting if you wrongly include the solid C(s) in equation 1. If you count C(s), you get 2 over 2 and predict no units, so you reject 1. Remember solids are never in Kc.
options.D: This suggests only 1 works. It is tempting if you think only an equation with a solid can change the units in this way. In fact equations 2 and 3 also have fewer product moles than reactant moles, so they give the same units.
